objectives: Recognize the use cases for CRDTs in practice.

slides.title: Consistency models — from linearizability to eventual consistency
slides.body:
Beyond CAP's 'C or A', consistency is a spectrum. Understanding the spectrum is the foundation for reasoning about distributed systems design.

- **Linearizability** (also called strong consistency or atomic consistency): every operation appears to take effect at a single indivisible point in time between its invocation and completion. Operations are totally-ordered and observable consistently from any client. Defined formally by **Maurice Herlihy** and **Jeannette Wing** in *"Linearizability: A Correctness Condition for Concurrent Objects"* (ACM TOPLAS, 1990). Linearizable systems include single-node ACID databases and distributed systems that achieve consensus (Zookeeper, etcd, Google Chubby).
- **Sequential consistency**: operations are totally ordered but the order need not match wall-clock time across clients. Weaker than linearizability; cheaper to implement. **Leslie Lamport** introduced sequential consistency in *"How to Make a Multiprocessor Computer That Correctly Executes Multiprocess Programs"* (IEEE TC, 1979).
- **Causal consistency**: causally related operations (A writes X, B reads X then writes Y) preserve their order everywhere; concurrent operations may be reordered. Defined rigorously in the context of distributed systems by **Mustaque Ahamad et al.** (1995). Captures real-world happens-before relationships without requiring total order.
- **Read-your-writes** (session consistency): a client always sees its own writes immediately, but may see stale reads of other clients' writes. Common in systems with sticky sessions or primary-replica routing.
- **Eventual consistency**: all replicas will eventually converge to the same state if no new updates are made. Intermediate states may be inconsistent. **Werner Vogels** (Amazon CTO) popularized the term in *"Eventually Consistent"* (ACM Queue, 2008 / CACM, 2009), describing how Amazon built large-scale systems on eventual consistency.

Production systems mix-and-match. A social-media feed might be eventually consistent (your friend's new post takes seconds to propagate); your own profile might be read-your-writes (you immediately see your own edits); a payment transaction must be linearizable.

The weaker the consistency model, the cheaper the system — fewer round trips, no need for quorum. Picking the strongest model your use case requires (not stronger) is the design discipline. **Amazon Dynamo** (2007), described in the paper *"Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-Value Store"* by **Giuseppe DeCandia, Deniz Hastorun, Madan Jampani**, and colleagues at Amazon, is the canonical example of an eventually consistent system: it uses consistent hashing, quorum reads/writes (W + R > N), and vector clocks for conflict detection, accepting that concurrent writes may require application-level reconciliation.

**Vector clocks** are the standard mechanism for tracking causality in distributed systems. Each node maintains a vector of logical timestamps, one per node. On write, the local component increments. On receive, components are element-wise maxed. Two events are causally related if one vector clock dominates the other; they are concurrent if neither dominates. **Leslie Lamport** introduced logical clocks in *"Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System"* (CACM, 1978); Colin Fidge and Friedemann Mattern independently developed vector clocks in 1988.

slides.title: CRDTs — conflict-free replicated data types
slides.body:
**Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs)** were formally introduced by **Marc Shapiro**, **Nuno Preguiça**, **Carlos Baquero**, and **Marek Zawirski** in the 2011 technical report *"A Comprehensive Study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types"* (INRIA RR-7506, 2011). The central insight: if you design your data structure so that merge is always defined, commutative, associative, and idempotent, then replicas will converge to the same state regardless of the order in which they receive updates — with no coordination required.

Formal structure: a CRDT's state space forms a **join-semilattice** — a partially ordered set in which every pair of elements has a least upper bound (the join, $\sqcup$). The merge operation is exactly the join. Monotonicity: states only move upward in the lattice; there is no rollback. This lattice structure is what guarantees **strong eventual consistency (SEC)**: all replicas that have received the same set of updates hold the same state.

**Two flavors:**

**State-based CRDTs (CvRDTs — convergent replicated data types)**: each replica periodically ships its entire state to other replicas; the receiving replica applies the merge (join) function. Requires that states be transmitted in full, but works even if messages are delivered multiple times (idempotent merge handles duplicates) or out of order (commutative + associative merge handles reordering).

**Operation-based CRDTs (CmRDTs — commutative replicated data types)**: each replica broadcasts the operation (not the full state) when it mutates. Requires that the delivery channel be reliable (each op delivered exactly once) and that operations commute. Smaller messages; harder delivery guarantee.

**Classic CRDT examples:**
- **G-Counter** (grow-only counter): per-replica integer vector. Replica $i$ increments only its slot $v[i]$. Merge: elementwise max. Total value: $\sum_i v[i]$. Trivially convergent because no two replicas write to the same slot.
- **PN-Counter** (positive-negative counter): two G-Counters — one for increments, one for decrements. Net value: $\text{sum}(P) - \text{sum}(N)$. Supports both increment and decrement.
- **OR-Set** (observed-remove set): add and remove with unique tags (typically UUIDs). Each add generates a fresh tag; remove deletes specific tags. Add and remove commute because they operate on disjoint tag sets. Resolves the add-wins vs remove-wins ambiguity by making concurrently added elements survive concurrent removes.
- **LWW-Register** (last-write-wins register): a single value with a timestamp. Merge: take the value with the higher timestamp. Simple; loses the losing write on concurrent updates. Used in **Apache Cassandra** for cells with `WRITETIME` semantics.
- **RGA (Replicated Growable Array)**: CRDT for ordered sequences (text). Used internally by **Automerge** and related systems. Handles concurrent insertions at the same position by assigning unique identifiers to positions.

**Strong eventual consistency (SEC)**, defined precisely by Shapiro et al., is stronger than plain eventual consistency: any two replicas that have delivered the same set of updates (in any order) are in identical states — not just eventually, but immediately. CRDTs are the class of data structures that satisfy SEC.

**Production deployments:**
- **Riak** (Basho): the first major database to ship built-in CRDT types — counters, sets, maps, registers, flags — replacing the earlier application-level reconciliation model. Documented in *"Riak Data Types"* (Basho, 2014).
- **Redis Enterprise** CRDT: active-active geo-distributed deployments using CRDT semantics for counters and sets across datacenters.
- **Automerge** (Martin Kleppmann et al.): a JSON-like document CRDT for collaborative editing. Used in local-first software architectures. Based on the **LSEQ** and **RGA** sequence CRDTs.
- **Yjs** (Kevin Jahns): a high-performance CRDT framework in JavaScript powering collaborative text in **Linear**, **Notion**, and many other editors. Uses the YATA (Yet Another Transformation Approach) algorithm.
- **Apple Notes** offline sync uses CRDT-like merge logic for note content.

slides.title: Worked example: Yjs in collaborative editors
slides.body:
Yjs (Y-CRDT in JavaScript) powers Linear, Notion, Trello, and many collaborative editors. State-based CRDT for text + nested data structures. Each client maintains local replica, broadcasts ops, merges replicas. No central server required for correctness (servers help with persistence + connectivity). The CRDT machinery guarantees: any subset of clients can disconnect + reconnect; documents converge once everyone sees the same ops in any order.

**Why CRDTs beat Operational Transformation (OT) for offline-first.** Google Docs uses **Operational Transformation (OT)** — a technique pioneered by **C. Ellis and S. Gibbs** in *"Concurrency Control in Groupware Systems"* (ACM SIGMOD, 1989). OT transforms operations against concurrent operations to preserve intent. It requires a central server to impose a total order on operations; without a central server, OT is notoriously difficult to implement correctly (**Joseph Gentle** called this out in the influential 2010 blog post "Operational Transformation is a Nightmare"). CRDTs do not require a central ordering authority, making them the natural fit for **local-first software** — a design philosophy articulated by **Martin Kleppmann, Adam Wiggins, Peter van Hardenberg, and Mark McGranaghan** in *"Local-First Software: You Own Your Data, in Spite of the Cloud"* (ACM ONWARD!, 2019).

**The semilattice in practice.** For a G-Counter with 3 replicas:
- State $s_A = \{A:5, B:0, C:2\}$, $s_B = \{A:3, B:7, C:2\}$.
- Merge: $s_A \sqcup s_B = \{A:\max(5,3), B:\max(0,7), C:\max(2,2)\} = \{A:5, B:7, C:2\}$.
- Total value: $5 + 7 + 2 = 14$.
- Applying the merge again (idempotent): same result. Applying in reverse order (commutative): same result.

**Limitations.** CRDTs are not universally applicable. Operations that require global constraints — "transfer money from account A to account B" (requires both to be updated atomically) or "reserve the last seat" (requires knowing the global count is still $>0$) — cannot be expressed as CRDTs without additional coordination. For these, distributed transactions (2PC, Percolator, Spanner) or the Saga pattern remain necessary. The art is identifying which operations genuinely commute and which require coordination.

question.question: Prove G-Counter convergence
question.goal: G-counter state: vector of per-replica counts. Merge: elementwise max. Show idempotent + commutative + associative.

steps.prompt: Idempotent: $\text{merge}(s, s) = s$? (Elementwise max of $s$ with itself.)

options: Yes: $\max(s_i, s_i) = s_i$ for each component.

steps.prompt: Commutative + associative? (Both follow from max's properties.)

options: Yes — max is commutative + associative, so elementwise extension is too.

hints: Componentwise extension of an associative + commutative operator inherits both.
steps.reveal: Yes. Merge is idempotent, commutative, associative → CRDT (state-based, CvRDT).

question.finalResult: Convergence: idempotent + commutative + associative → all replicas converge to the same state given the same set of merges, regardless of order. The CRDT lattice property.

question.question: A G-Counter has two replicas. Replica A's local count: 5. Replica B's local count: 7. After they merge (elementwise max of the per-replica vectors {A: 5, B: 0} and {A: 0, B: 7}), the total counter value is:
question.explanation: G-Counter state is per-replica: each replica counts its own increments. The total counter value is the sum across replicas. Vector ${A: 5, B: 0} \sqcup {A: 0, B: 7} = {A: 5, B: 7}$ — elementwise max. Total = 5 + 7 = 12. Merge is commutative + associative + idempotent — exactly the CRDT requirements.

hints: G-Counter stores per-replica counts; total is the sum.
Each replica only increments its OWN slot; merge takes the max per slot.
slides.workedSolution: G-Counter: each replica $i$ stores its own count $c_i$; total = $\sum_i c_i$. Merge: elementwise max of the count vectors. Replica A: ${A:5, B:0}$; Replica B: ${A:0, B:7}$. Merged: ${A:5, B:7}$. Total: 12. Correct because each replica only increments its own slot — no two replicas write to the same slot, so max equals 'take whichever has incremented more', which is the right thing.

question.question: Where CRDTs shine
question.prompt: A real-time collaborative text editor (think Google Docs) needs to handle simultaneous edits from multiple users with offline support. Why is a CRDT (or operational-transform) the dominant technical approach, and what's the tradeoff vs server-mediated coordination?
Explain in two or three sentences when CRDTs are the right tool and when they aren't.
question.rubric: Mentions that CRDTs are great for eventually-consistent collaboration on operations expressible as commutative merges; arbitrary operations (e.g., 'transfer money', 'reserve seat') don't fit and need stronger coordination; the right tool is matched to the operation's required consistency.
